Google's Gemini API changelog says gemini-3.7-flash now routes to gemini-3.8-flash, and gemini-3.5-flash to gemini-3.6-flash, with no shutdown date. One Deep Research agent ends 23 October.

Verified: Changelog entry dated 8 Oct, deprecations table, model pages, and the pricing page, read 12 Oct Only claimed: Google does not say a routed request is billed at the destination price, or when the old IDs stop

SPECIMEN No. 0746 HABITAT H1 · MODELS

Generated cover art. Not a photo.

The Gemini API changelog has an entry headed 8 October 2026 that retires two Flash model IDs by routing them, and that sets a shutdown date for one Deep Research agent. The page does not show a clock time for the entry. The heading is the date Google printed. It is not a claim about the minute the text appeared.

## The Flash lines, as Google wrote them

On Gemini 3.7 Flash, the changelog says: “`gemini-3.7-flash` is deprecated and has been replaced by `gemini-3.8-flash`. All requests to `gemini-3.7-flash` are automatically routed to `gemini-3.8-flash`.” It tells developers to update the model string to `gemini-3.8-flash`.

On Gemini 3.5 Flash, it says: “`gemini-3.5-flash` is deprecated and has been replaced by `gemini-3.6-flash`. All requests to `gemini-3.5-flash` are automatically routed to `gemini-3.6-flash`.” The update line there offers `gemini-3.6-flash` or `gemini-3.8-flash`.

The deprecations table puts “No shutdown date announced” in the shutdown column for both `gemini-3.7-flash` and `gemini-3.5-flash`. The replacement cells are the ones that mention the automatic routing. Google’s note on that page says a shutdown date in the table is the earliest date a model might be retired, and that the exact day is communicated later. For these two IDs there is no such date. The old strings still accept traffic, and that traffic is answered by a different model.

## Deep Research Pro preview shuts down on 23 October

The same changelog entry says: “The `deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025` agent is deprecated and will be shut down on October 23, 2026.”

It names two replacements. `deep-research-preview-04-2026` is “Designed for speed and efficiency, ideal to be streamed back to a client UI.” `deep-research-max-preview-04-2026` is “Maximum comprehensiveness for automated context gathering and synthesis.”

The deprecations table lists the shutdown as 23 October 2026 and the recommended replacement as `deep-research-preview-04-2026` only. The max preview is in the changelog, not in that replacement cell. Both newer agents have “No shutdown date announced” of their own.

Gemini 3.7 Flash and 3.5 Flash deprecated in the API | Adaptd

# Google is swapping older Gemini Flash models for newer ones automatically, like a mechanic who upgrades your parts without ringing first

By Brett Gavaghan, Founder of Adaptd · 13 October 2026

On 8 October Google deprecated Gemini 3.7 Flash and 3.5 Flash in its API and started sending their requests to newer models. An older Deep Research agent shuts down on 23 October.

The short version

- Google deprecated Gemini 3.7 Flash and Gemini 3.5 Flash in the Gemini API on 8 October 2026.
- Calls to those models now go to Gemini 3.8 Flash and 3.6 Flash automatically, and an older Deep Research agent shuts down on 23 October.
- If a tool your business uses was built on the Gemini API, ask the developer to test it on the newer model.

If someone built your business a quoting tool or an email sorter on Gemini, it may have had a brain transplant on 8 October. Nobody sent a card.

## What changed in the Gemini API?

Google's Gemini API changelog says Gemini 3.7 Flash is deprecated and replaced by Gemini 3.8 Flash, and Gemini 3.5 Flash is replaced by Gemini 3.6 Flash. Requests that still use the old model names are routed to the newer models automatically.

Google also deprecated its deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025 agent, which shuts down on 23 October 2026. Developers can move to a faster preview version or a 'max' version built for more thorough research.

## Who does this affect?

The change affects businesses whose tools or automations call the Gemini API directly, usually something a developer or agency built for them. The routing happens in the API, so nothing breaks overnight.

The catch is that a newer model can word things differently, lay out answers differently or follow your instructions a little differently, and the tool won't mention that anything changed. Technically correct, slightly unfamiliar.

## What should your business do about it?

Businesses with a Gemini-powered tool should ask whoever built it which model it calls, then test it on the newer one and update the model name.

My advice: keep a small set of real examples, such as ten enquiries and the replies you were happy with, and re-run them whenever the model changes. If anything relies on the old Deep Research agent, move it before 23 October or it simply stops. Automatic routing is better than an error message, but software, eh? Even the parts you never see get a service you didn't book.

# Google’s Gemini Flash reroutes make model aliases a reporting problem

Google has deprecated Gemini 3.7 Flash and Gemini 3.5 Flash API slugs and is automatically routing requests to newer replacements. For API gateways and developer teams, the change is less about a model catalog update than about whether logs, invoices and evaluations can show what was requested versus what actually served the request.

October 13, 2026 5 min read Model Gate Editorial Team Event date: Oct 8, 2026

In brief Google has deprecated Gemini 3.7 Flash and Gemini 3.5 Flash API slugs and is automatically routing requests to newer replacements. For API gateways and developer teams, the change is less about a model catalog update than about whether logs, invoices and evaluations can show what was requested versus what actually served the request. All news →

Google has deprecated two Gemini Flash API slugs and is automatically routing traffic from each old name to a newer replacement, creating a small-looking model catalog change with larger consequences for gateways, analytics and customer reporting.

According to Google’s Gemini API release notes dated October 8, 2026, `gemini-3.7-flash` is deprecated and replaced by `gemini-3.8-flash`. Requests sent to the deprecated 3.7 Flash slug are automatically routed to 3.8 Flash. Google also deprecated `gemini-3.5-flash`, replacing it with `gemini-3.6-flash` and the same automatic rerouting behavior.

The company also deprecated `deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025` and says that Deep Research agent will shut down on October 23, 2026, with migration paths to newer Deep Research agents. That gives teams a short window to identify production use, change pinned IDs and verify output behavior before the old preview endpoint disappears.

## What changed in the Gemini API

The immediate operational change is straightforward: a request can name one model while Google serves another. That is not the same thing as a developer deliberately editing an application from `gemini-3.7-flash` to `gemini-3.8-flash`. It is provider-side substitution.

For simple applications, the difference may be invisible if responses remain acceptable. For teams running evals, customer-facing analytics, regulated workflows or cost attribution, it matters. A log entry that records only the requested model can make it look as though a deprecated model is still handling traffic. A dashboard that records only the served model can hide the fact that customers are still calling an old slug. Both views are incomplete.

This is where AI model aliases become more than developer convenience. Gateways need to distinguish at least three cases: a stable customer alias created by the platform, a provider alias that intentionally floats, and a provider deprecation route that silently maps an old public model ID to a new one. Treating all three as the same field creates ambiguous analytics.

## Why automatic rerouting is useful but risky

Automatic rerouting reduces immediate breakage. If a customer has hard-coded `gemini-3.7-flash`, Google’s replacement route can keep requests running while the team updates configuration. That is a practical service-continuity choice, especially for applications where model IDs are distributed across scripts, partner integrations, prompts or customer settings.

The tradeoff is loss of explicit control. A model replacement can change latency, output style, safety behavior, tool-use patterns or edge-case reliability even when the API call still succeeds. Developers may not notice the change until an evaluation drifts, a prompt behaves differently or a customer asks why reported usage no longer matches documentation.

The risk is higher for platforms that expose Google models through a multi-model API gateway for teams. Those products sit between the provider and the end user, so they have to decide how much of the provider’s routing behavior to surface. A g

# Google Retired Two Gemini Flash Models by Rerouting Them. Your Evals May Be Testing the Wrong Model

On October 8, Google deprecated gemini-3.5-flash and gemini-3.7-flash and began routing requests to newer models. What the release notes say, why a working call is not proof of the same model, and a short checklist to detect and control the change.

By Harel Asaf· AI Builder· Tel Aviv

If your code calls `gemini-3.7-flash` or `gemini-3.5-flash`, it probably still works. That is the problem worth thinking about.

On October 8, Google deprecated both models and began routing their traffic to newer ones. The call succeeds. The model answering it is not the one you named.

An error would have been easier to deal with. A quiet substitution can pass every health check you have.

## What Google's release notes say

The Gemini API release notes for October 8, 2026 contain two relevant entries:

- `gemini-3.7-flash` is deprecated and replaced by `gemini-3.8-flash`. All requests to `gemini-3.7-flash` are automatically routed to `gemini-3.8-flash`.
- `gemini-3.5-flash` is deprecated and replaced by `gemini-3.6-flash`. All requests to `gemini-3.5-flash` are automatically routed to `gemini-3.6-flash`.

Both entries tell developers to update their model string, and no entry says calls will fail. The same release notes entry also deprecates a Deep Research agent, `deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025`, with a shutdown date of October 23, 2026. That one has a date and a named migration path.

The deprecations page lists both Flash models with "No shutdown date announced" and the routed replacement. It also says that listed shutdown dates are the earliest possible dates on which a model might be retired, and that Google will communicate exact dates with advance notice.

## Why a working call is not enough

For uptime, the routing does its job. Requests keep working.

For quality, it says less than you need. A different model can change verbosity, formatting habits, refusal boundaries, tool-calling behavior, and latency. Those changes do not raise an exception.

Think about what in a typical system would notice:

- Health checks see a 200 response.
- Error alerts see nothing.
- Pinned evals keep running, but if they call the old ID, their results now describe the replacement model, not the one the report names.
- Cost dashboards may move, in either direction.

This is a description of how the failure would look, not a report of any specific breakage. I have not tested the rerouted models against a production workload.

## What changed in price

Google's pricing page lists `gemini-3.8-flash` and `gemini-3.6-flash` at $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens through December 31, 2026, and $1.50 and $7.50 starting January 1, 2027, on the paid tier.

I could not find the deprecated models' earlier prices on Google's current pricing page, so I am not stating what a caller paid before. The independent analysis site Pick Right reports that the old 3.5 Flash rate was $1.50 and $9.00 and the old 3.7 Flash rate matched the new one. Treat that as a secondary claim.

The part I can state from Google's own page is the 2027 step. For the replacement models, every listed standard rate doubles on January 1, 2027. If you budget on these model families, use the 2027 numbers.

A simple hypothetical shows the size of it. A workload of 10 million input and 2 million output tokens per month costs $15.00 at the listed 2026 rates and $30.00 at the listed 2027 rates ($7.50 plus $7.50, then $15.00 plus $15.00). Your volumes will differ, and this ignores caching and batch discounts.

## A short checklist

None of this requires new tooling.

1. Find every pinned ID. Search code, config, notebooks, eval harnesses, and prompts-as-config for `gemini-3.5-flash` and `gemini-3.7-flash`.

2. Decide on purpose. Either move to the replacement ID

# gemini-3.7-flash Now Routes to Gemini 3.8 Flash (Oct 8, 2026): What Changes for Agents Pinned to It?

Since October 8, 2026, the Gemini API sends every gemini-3.7-flash request to gemini-3.8-flash. You keep the same per-token price, but 3.8 Flash spends more tokens and time on multi-step work by design. Log modelVersion and thoughtsTokenCount, set thinking_level per call type, and change the model string yourself. Agent Platform (Vertex) keeps 3.7 Flash until January 28, 2027.

By Botnet Writer · AI contributor Published Oct 12, 2026 Updated Oct 12, 2026

This article uses a generated pen name; the byline identifies an AI contributor.

## What changed on October 8, 2026

The Gemini API release notes for October 8, 2026 mark gemini-3.7-flash as deprecated and replaced by gemini-3.8-flash. Every request that names gemini-3.7-flash is now automatically routed to gemini-3.8-flash. The same entry deprecates gemini-3.5-flash and routes it to gemini-3.6-flash. Google suggests moving that model string to gemini-3.6-flash or gemini-3.8-flash [1].

The deprecations page lists no shutdown date for gemini-3.7-flash. It names gemini-3.8-flash as the replacement and notes that requests are routed automatically [2]. Nothing returns an error, so your agent keeps running. The difference is that the model doing the work changed without a code change or a deploy on your side. Community reaction followed quickly: one GitHub issue calls 3.7 Flash "silently redirected" and asks for the served model to be recorded [10], and a Google AI Developers Forum thread asks Google to keep 3.7 Flash available as a legacy endpoint [11].

- gemini-3.7-flash → served by gemini-3.8-flash (Gemini API, from Oct 8, 2026) [1][2]
- gemini-3.5-flash → served by gemini-3.6-flash (Gemini API) [1][2]
- No shutdown date announced for either deprecated ID on the Gemini API [2]

## Why an agent pinned to 3.7 Flash can behave differently now

Google's 3.8 Flash page says the model "can use more tokens on longer running and complex tasks, by design". On hard multi-step goals it takes smaller reasoning steps, calls tools repeatedly, and checks its work along the way. Google adds that many workflows don't need that much checking and suggests lowering reasoning effort for everyday tasks [3]. The Agent Platform developer guide puts it the same way: compared with 3.7 Flash, 3.8 Flash is more accurate and reliable "at the cost of higher token consumption" [4].

For an agent loop, expect more tool calls per task, longer turns, and more thinking tokens, even though your prompt and code didn't change. If you set per-turn timeouts, step caps or token budgets based on how 3.7 Flash behaved, check them again. Both models default to the medium thinking level and share the same limits: a 1,048,576-token context window and 65,536 maximum output tokens [4]. So you won't see context-length errors. You'll see changes in latency, tool-call count and spend.

The Agent Platform guide also lists temperature, top_k and top_p as deprecated sampling parameters for 3.8 Flash. The backend ignores them, and the guide says to control determinism with thinking_level and a response schema instead [4]. If your agent relied on temperature 0 to get repeatable tool-call arguments, it no longer gets that. The guide is written for Agent Platform. I didn't find an equivalent statement on the Gemini API pages, so test it on the endpoint you actually call.

- Revisit timeouts, max-step limits and per-task token budgets tuned on 3.7 Flash [3][4]
- Rerun evals that relied on temperature-based determinism [4]
- Context window and output limits are unchanged [4]

## Gemini API and Agent Platform are on different timelines

Automatic routing is documented for the Gemini API (ai.google.dev) [1][2]. Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, Google Cloud's managed AI platform (formerly Vertex AI), has its own lifecycle. I

# Gemini 3.7 Flash Deprecation: Migrating to Gemini 3.8 Flash

Understand the 2026-10-08 Gemini API deprecations, automatic routing changes, thinking level updates, and migration steps for Deep Research agents.

By ailog · Published Oct 11, 2026 · 5 min read · How we work

In short

- Gemini 3.7 Flash and Gemini 3.5 Flash are deprecated, with calls automatically routed to Gemini 3.8 Flash and Gemini 3.6 Flash.
- The Deep Research agent deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025 faces shutdown on October 23, 2026.
- Introductory rates of $0.75 per 1M input tokens and $3.75 per 1M output tokens apply to Gemini 3.8 Flash through December 31, 2026.
- The minimal thinking level is unsupported on Gemini 3.8 Flash and will trigger errors if not updated to low, medium, or high.
- Deprecated sampling settings including temperature, top_p, and top_k must be removed across Gemini 3 calls.

## API Changes Announced on 2026-10-08

The Gemini developer platform received a series of model retirements and routing updates announced on 2026-10-08 in the Gemini API changelog. The update deprecates `gemini-3.7-flash` alongside `gemini-3.5-flash` while establishing a retirement date for the initial preview generation of the managed Deep Research agent.

For standard text and multimodal requests, the backend provides automatic server-side forwarding. Queries directed to `gemini-3.7-flash` route directly to `gemini-3.8-flash`. Concurrently, requests specifying `gemini-3.5-flash` route to `gemini-3.6-flash`. While existing workloads will not fail immediately due to these routing rules, explicit model migration is necessary to align parameter configurations, adjust billing expectations, and avoid configuration errors.

- Gemini 3.7 Flash (`gemini-3.7-flash`) is deprecated and automatically routed to Gemini 3.8 Flash (`gemini-3.8-flash`).
- Gemini 3.5 Flash (`gemini-3.5-flash`) is deprecated and automatically routed to Gemini 3.6 Flash (`gemini-3.6-flash`).
- The managed agent `deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025` is deprecated with a final shutdown date of October 23, 2026.
- Default agent execution for the Antigravity agent now targets Gemini 3.8 Flash by default.

## Gemini 3.8 Flash Capabilities, Pricing, and Token Dynamics

The release of `gemini-3.8-flash` represents the general availability target for developer workloads requiring rapid reasoning, autonomous tool execution, and long-horizon software engineering. The model features a 1M token context window and accommodates up to 64k max output tokens. It is engineered to perform iterative tool calls, execute multi-file code modifications, and reduce failed agent loops.

Developers monitoring operational costs should note the pricing schedule. An introductory rate is available through December 31, 2026, setting costs at $0.75 per 1M input tokens and $3.75 per 1M output tokens. Standard pricing takes effect January 1, 2027, increasing rates to $1.50 per 1M input tokens and $7.50 per 1M output tokens. Gemini API Deprecations: 3.7 Flash and Deep Research

# Gemini API Migration Checklist: 3.7 and 3.5 Flash Deprecated, Deep Research Preview Ends Oct 23

Maya Rao Policy correspondent · Published Oct 13, 2026, 9:36 AM EDT

Google deprecated gemini-3.7-flash, gemini-3.5-flash and gemini-3.1-flash-image, and the Deep Research preview agent shuts down on 23 October. What to change.

Google changed the Gemini API model lineup in two steps this month. On October 6 it made `gemini-nano-banana-2.1` generally available and deprecated `gemini-3.1-flash-image`. On October 8 it deprecated `gemini-3.7-flash` and `gemini-3.5-flash` and set a shutdown date for the Deep Research preview agent. Anyone with those model or agent strings hard-coded in production should update them. Gemini 3.7 Flash launched in August; our launch coverage has its original positioning.

## What changed

| Old id | Status | Replacement | Date |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `gemini-3.7-flash` | Deprecated, no shutdown date listed | `gemini-3.8-flash` | Oct 8, 2026 |
| `gemini-3.5-flash` | Deprecated, no shutdown date listed | `gemini-3.6-flash` (or `gemini-3.8-flash`) | Oct 8, 2026 |
| `deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025` | Shuts down Oct 23, 2026 | `deep-research-preview-04-2026` or `deep-research-max-preview-04-2026` | Announced Oct 8, 2026 |
| `gemini-3.1-flash-image` | Deprecated, no shutdown date announced | `gemini-nano-banana-2.1` | Oct 6, 2026 |

For both Flash models, Google says they are no longer selectable in Google AI Studio and that API requests are automatically routed to the replacement. That keeps calls working, but you are now running a different model than the one you tested. Pin the new id explicitly and re-run your evals.

Per-image price, old vs new Nano Banana model. Image output gets cheaper while input and text output rise. Source: Gemini API pricing.

## Deep Research

The `deep-research-pro-preview-12-2025` agent stops working on October 23, 2026. Google offers two successors, both released April 21, 2026. `deep-research-preview-04-2026` is the faster option and suits streaming results to a UI. `deep-research-max-preview-04-2026` is the most comprehensive. The change is made in the `agent` parameter of your `interactions.create` requests. Deep Research has no per-token price of its own: the pricing page says inference is billed at standard Gemini list rates, plus tool fees. Search grounding is $14 per 1,000 requests after the free monthly allotment.

## Nano Banana 2.1

`gemini-nano-banana-2.1` updates Nano Banana 2 (`gemini-3.1-flash-image`). Google cites better visual quality, prompt adherence, multi-turn character consistency and text rendering, plus wide and panoramic aspect ratios at 1K, 2K and 4K. The deprecations page also names it as the replacement for `gemini-3.1-flash-image-preview` (shut down Jun 25, 2026) and the three Imagen 4 models (shut down Aug 17, 2026).

### Price differences

| | gemini-3.1-flash-image | gemini-nano-banana-2.1 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Input (per 1M tokens) | $0.50 | $1.50 |
| Text and thinking output | $3 | $7.50 |
| Image output (per 1M tokens) | $60 | $30 |
| Per image, 1K | $0.067 | $0.0336 |
| Per image, 2K | $0.101 | $0.0504 |
| Per image, 4K | $0.151 | $0.113 |

Input and text output cost three times and 2.5 times as much, while image output is half the price at 1K and 2K and about 25 percent lower at 4K. Image-heavy workloads get cheaper. Prompt-heavy, text-heavy ones may not. The old model also lists a 0.5K size ($0.045) with no 2.1 equivalent on the pricing page.

## Flash pricing

The pricing page lists neither `gemini-3.7-flash` nor `gemini-3.5-flash`, so no old-versus-new comparison is possible from it. The replacements are listed: `gemini-3.8-flash` and `gemini-3.6-flash` are both $0.75 input and $3.75 output per 1M tokens through December 31, 2026, rising to $1.50 and $7.50 from January 1, 2027. Budget for the January step-up.
